Apple has submitted its proposal regarding the fees it can charge for transactions outside the App Store system in the Epic Games case. Details below.

Apple submits proposal for non-App Store commission rates

After multiple requests to stay the district court proceedings — which would determine what fees, if any, Apple can charge for transactions outside its App Store IAP system — Apple has now submitted its proposal for the rate structure.

Apple's submission comes as the Supreme Court has rejected its request to stay the lower court proceedings. The Supreme Court is currently considering whether Apple can be held in contempt for charging a 27% commission on transactions outside the App Store, in relation to an injunction issued by Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers that requires Apple to allow developers to direct users to alternative purchasing methods.

Apple argued in the lower court, and subsequently at the Supreme Court, that the Supreme Court's ruling could affect the outcome of the rate determination proceedings, and that those proceedings should therefore be paused until the Supreme Court issues its ruling. However, the Supreme Court rejected Apple's request, allowing the lower court proceedings to continue while the case is being heard.

Consequently, Apple has now submitted its proposal, which recommends the following:

Standard applications (subject to the 30% In-App Purchase ("IAP") commission) at 15%; Video Partner Program ("VPP"), News Partner Program ("NPP"), Mini Apps Partner Program ("MPP"), and subscription renewals at 10%; applications under the Small Business Program at 5%.

Apple stated that "factual and expert evidence regarding the proposed commission rates has been submitted concurrently." The company added:

Apple also stated that its "proposed outbound referral commissions can also be compared with commissions charged by other app stores competing with the App Store," including Google Play, the Samsung Galaxy Store, and Amazon's Android App Marketplace.

The company also noted that "Google Play charges a 'standard' rate of 20%, a programme rate of 15%, and a subscription rate of 10% for outbound referrals — rates to which Epic has also agreed."

Apple said it still believes the rate determination proceedings should be paused while the case is before the Supreme Court, and noted that submitting the proposal is solely to comply with Judge Gonzalez Rogers's instructions.

The company also mentioned that the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals has overturned the district court's blanket injunction on commissions for outbound referral transactions, ruling that such commissions are only problematic if they actually have a chilling effect.

With the proposal submitted, Epic will have an opportunity to respond, and Apple is expected to file its brief with the Supreme Court by September 14.
